title: The Story of the Youth Who Went Forth to Learn What Fear Was
paragraphs: A certain father had two sons. The elder was clever and sensible and could do anything, but the younger was stupid and couldn’t learn or understand a thing. When people saw him, they said, “That one will be a burden to his father!” Whenever there was work to be done, the elder son had to do it all. But if the father sent him for something late in the day, or in the middle of the night, and the way led through the churchyard or some other gloomy place, the younger would answer, “Oh no, father, I won’t go there. It makes me shudder!” He was afraid. And when stories were told by the fire at night that made people’s flesh creep, the listeners would often say, “Oh, it makes us shudder!” The younger son sat in his corner listening along with the rest and couldn’t imagine what they meant. “They keep saying, ‘It makes me shudder, it makes me shudder!’ It doesn’t make me shudder,” he thought. “That must be another skill I know nothing about!”

One day his father said to him, “Listen, you there in the corner. You’re getting big and strong, and you have to learn something to earn your living. Look how hard your brother works, while you don’t even earn your salt.” “Well, father,” he replied, “I’m quite willing to learn something. In fact, if it could be arranged, I’d like to learn how to shudder. I don’t understand that at all yet.” The elder brother smiled when he heard this and thought, “Good heavens, what a blockhead my brother is! He’ll never amount to anything as long as he lives! If you want to be a sickle, you have to start bending young.”
The father sighed and answered, “You’ll soon find out what it is to shudder, but you won’t earn a living by it.”

Soon afterward the sexton came to the house for a visit, and the father poured out his troubles, telling him how backward his younger son was in every way, knowing nothing and learning nothing. “Imagine,” he said, “when I asked him how he planned to earn his bread, he actually said he wanted to learn to shudder.” “If that’s all,” said the sexton, “he can learn it with me. Send him to me, and I’ll soon knock the rough edges off him.” The father was glad to agree, thinking, “It will do the boy some good.” So the sexton took him into his house, and the boy’s job was to ring the church bell. A day or two later, the sexton woke him at midnight and told him to get up, climb the church tower, and ring the bell. “You’ll soon learn what shuddering is,” the sexton thought. He slipped off secretly ahead of the boy. When the boy reached the top of the tower, turned around, and was about to take hold of the bell rope, he saw a white figure standing on the stairs across from the sounding hole. “Who’s there?” he called, but the figure gave no answer and didn’t move or stir. “Answer,” the boy called, “or get out of here. You have no business being here at night.”

The sexton, though, stood perfectly still so that the boy would take him for a ghost. The boy called out a second time, “What do you want here? Speak if you’re an honest man, or I’ll throw you down the steps!” The sexton thought, “He can’t mean it as badly as he says,” and he made no sound, standing as if he were made of stone. The boy called to him a third time, and when that did no good either, he charged at him and shoved the ghost down the stairs. It tumbled down ten steps and lay in a corner. Then the boy rang the bell, went home, and without a word got into bed and fell asleep. The sexton’s wife waited a long time for her husband, but he didn’t come back. At last she grew worried and woke the boy. “Do you know where my husband is?” she asked. “He went up the tower ahead of you.” “No, I don’t,” said the boy. “But someone was standing by the sounding hole across from the steps, and since he wouldn’t answer and wouldn’t go away, I took him for a scoundrel and threw him downstairs. Go and look, and you’ll see whether it was him. I’d be sorry if it was.” The woman ran off and found her husband lying in the corner, groaning. His leg was broken.

She carried him down, and then, screaming loudly, she hurried to the boy’s father. “Your boy,” she cried, “has caused a terrible disaster! He threw my husband down the steps and broke his leg. Get that good-for-nothing out of our house!” The father was horrified. He ran over and scolded the boy. “What wicked tricks are these?” he said. “The devil must have put them in your head.” “Father,” the boy replied, “please listen to me. I’m completely innocent. He was standing there in the night like someone planning something evil. I didn’t know who it was, and I begged him three times to either speak or leave.” “Ah,” said the father, “you bring me nothing but misery. Get out of my sight. I never want to see you again.”

“Yes, father, gladly. Just wait until daylight. Then I’ll go out and learn how to shudder, and at least I’ll have one skill to support me.” “Learn whatever you like,” said the father. “It’s all the same to me. Here are fifty talers. Take them and go out into the wide world, and don’t tell anyone where you come from or who your father is, because I have good reason to be ashamed of you.” “Yes, father, I’ll do as you say. If that’s all you ask, I can easily remember it.”

So when day broke, the boy put his fifty talers in his pocket and set out along the high road, saying to himself over and over, “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” A man approached and overheard the youth talking to himself. When they had walked a bit farther, to a place where the gallows came into view, the man said to him, “Look, there’s the tree where seven men married the ropemaker’s daughter and are now learning to fly. Sit down under it and wait for night, and you’ll soon learn how to shudder.” “If that’s all it takes,” the youth answered, “it’s easily done. But if I learn to shudder that fast, you can have my fifty talers. Come back to me early in the morning.” The youth went to the gallows, sat down beneath it, and waited for evening. He was cold, so he built himself a fire. But at midnight the wind blew so hard that even with the fire he couldn’t get warm. The wind knocked the hanged men against one another, swinging them back and forth, and he thought, “If you’re shivering down here by the fire, how those up there must freeze and suffer!” Feeling sorry for them, he set up the ladder, climbed up, untied them one after another, and brought all seven down. Then he stirred up the fire, blew on it, and sat them all around it to warm themselves. But they sat there without moving, and the fire caught their clothes. So he said, “Be careful, or I’ll hang you up again.” The dead men didn’t hear him. They stayed silent and let their rags go on burning. That made him angry. “If you won’t be careful, I can’t help you,” he said. “I’m not going to burn along with you.” And he hung them up again, one by one. Then he sat down by his fire and fell asleep. The next morning the man came and wanted his fifty talers. “Well, do you know how to shudder now?” he asked. “No,” the youth answered. “How would I? Those fellows up there never opened their mouths, and they were so stupid they let the few old rags on their backs burn up.” The man saw that he wouldn’t get the fifty talers that day, and he went away saying, “I’ve never met a youth like this before.”

The young man moved on too, and again muttered to himself: “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” A wagon driver walking close behind heard him and asked, “Who are you?” “I don’t know,” said the young man. “Where are you from?” “I don’t know that either.” “Who is your father?” “I’m not allowed to tell you.” “And what is it you keep mumbling under your breath?” “Oh,” the young man answered, “I want so badly to shudder, but nobody can teach me how.” “Enough of that silly talk,” said the driver. “Come along with me, and I’ll see about a place for you.” The young man went with him, and that evening they reached an inn where they meant to spend the night. In the doorway of the taproom the young man said again, quite loudly, “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” The innkeeper heard it and laughed. “If that’s what you want,” he said, “you’ll find a fine chance for it here.” “Oh, hush,” said the innkeeper’s wife. “Plenty of nosy people have lost their lives already. It would be a pity and a shame if a pair of eyes as lovely as these never saw daylight again.”

But the young man said, “However hard it is, I’m going to learn it. That’s the very reason I set out from home.” He gave the innkeeper no peace until the man told him that not far away stood a haunted castle, where anyone could easily find out what shuddering was, if only he would keep watch there for three nights. The king had promised his daughter in marriage to anyone who dared to try, and she was the loveliest girl the sun ever shone on. The castle also held great treasures, guarded by evil spirits. Those treasures would be freed, and would make a poor man rich enough. Many men had already gone into the castle, but so far none had come out again. So the next morning the young man went to the king and said, “With your permission, I will gladly keep watch for three nights in the haunted castle.”

The king looked him over, and since he liked the young man, he said, “You may ask for three things to take into the castle with you, but they must be things that have no life.” He answered, “Then I ask for a fire, a lathe, and a carving bench with its knife.”

During the day the king had these things carried into the castle. As night came on, the young man went up and built himself a bright fire in one of the rooms. He set the carving bench and knife beside it and sat down at the lathe. “Oh, if only I could shudder!” he said. “But I won’t learn it here either.” Toward midnight he was about to stir up his fire, and as he was blowing on it, something suddenly cried out from a corner: “Meow, meow! We’re so cold!” “You fools!” he called. “What are you howling about? If you’re cold, come over, sit by the fire and warm yourselves.” No sooner had he said it than two huge black cats came bounding over in one great leap. They sat down on either side of him and glared at him wildly with their fiery eyes. After a little while, when they had warmed up, they said, “Friend, shall we play a game of cards?” “Why not?” he answered. “But first let me see your paws.” They stretched out their claws. “My,” he said, “what long nails you have! Hold on, I have to trim them for you first.” With that he grabbed them by the neck, laid them on the carving bench and clamped their paws tight. “I’ve taken a good look at your fingers,” he said, “and I’ve lost all taste for cards.” Then he beat them to death and threw them out into the water. But when he had finished off those two and was about to sit down by his fire again, black cats and black dogs with red-hot chains came swarming out of every hole and corner. More and more of them came, until he could not move. They howled dreadfully, jumped onto his fire, scattered it and tried to put it out. For a while he watched them calmly, but at last, when they were going too far, he grabbed his carving knife and shouted, “Get away, you vermin!” and started cutting them down. Some ran off, and the rest he killed and threw into the fish pond. When he came back, he blew the embers of his fire back to life and warmed himself. As he sat there, his eyes refused to stay open any longer, and he felt like sleeping. He looked around and saw a big bed in a corner. “Just what I need,” he said, and climbed in. But just as he was about to close his eyes, the bed began to move by itself and rolled through the whole castle. “Good,” he said. “Now go faster.” The bed raced along as though six horses were pulling it, up and down, over doorsills and stairs. Then suddenly, hop, hop, it flipped upside down and lay on top of him like a mountain. He heaved the quilts and pillows into the air, crawled out and said, “Now whoever wants to can do the driving.” He lay down by his fire and slept until daylight. In the morning the king arrived, and seeing him stretched out on the floor, he thought the evil spirits had killed him and that he was dead. “What a shame,” he said, “for such a handsome man.” The young man heard this, got up and said, “It hasn’t come to that yet.” The king was amazed, but very glad, and asked how he had fared. “Very well indeed,” he answered. “One night is over, and the other two will pass the same way.” Then he went to the innkeeper, who stared at him wide-eyed. “I never expected to see you alive again,” the man said. “Have you learned to shudder yet?” “No,” said the young man, “it’s all for nothing. If only somebody would tell me how!”

On the second night he went up into the old castle again, sat down by the fire and started in on his old refrain: “If only I could shudder!” At midnight a racket began, a noise of things tumbling around. It was soft at first, then grew louder and louder. After a quiet spell, half a man came down the chimney with a loud scream and dropped in front of him. “Hey!” he cried. “There’s another half that goes with that. This isn’t enough!” Then the racket started up again, with roaring and howling, and the other half fell down as well. “Wait,” he said, “I’ll build up the fire a bit for you.” When he had done so and looked around again, the two pieces had joined together, and a hideous man was sitting in his seat. “That wasn’t part of our deal,” said the young man. “The bench is mine.” The man tried to shove him off, but the young man would not stand for it. He pushed the man away with all his strength and sat back down in his own place. Then more men dropped down one after another. They had brought nine dead men’s legs and two skulls, and they set them up and played ninepins with them. The young man wanted to play too and said, “Say, can I join you?” “Yes, if you have money.” “Money enough,” he replied, “but your balls aren’t quite round.” He took the skulls, put them in the lathe and turned them until they were round. “There, now they’ll roll better!” he said. “Hooray! Now we’ll have some fun!” He played along and lost some of his money, but when the clock struck twelve, everything vanished from his sight. He lay down and went quietly to sleep. The next morning the king came to ask about him. “How did it go this time?” he asked. “I was playing ninepins,” the young man answered, “and I lost a couple of farthings.” “Didn’t you shudder, then?” “What?” he said. “I had a wonderful time! If only I knew what it was to shudder!”

On the third night he sat down on his bench again and said, quite gloomily, “If only I could shudder.” When it was late, six tall men came in carrying a coffin. “Ha, ha,” he said, “that must be my little cousin, who died just a few days ago.” He crooked his finger and called, “Come, little cousin, come here.” They set the coffin on the floor. He went over, took off the lid, and a dead man lay inside. He touched the face, and it was cold as ice. “Wait,” he said, “I’ll warm you up a little.” He went to the fire, warmed his hand and laid it on the dead man’s face, but the man stayed cold. So he lifted him out, sat down by the fire, set him on his chest and rubbed his arms to get the blood moving again. When that did no good either, he thought, “When two people lie in bed together, they warm each other.” He carried the dead man to the bed, covered him up and lay down beside him. After a while the dead man grew warm too and began to stir. “You see, little cousin,” said the young man, “didn’t I warm you up?” But the dead man got up and cried, “Now I’m going to strangle you.”

“What!” said the young man. “Is that how you thank me? Back into your coffin you go!” He picked him up, threw him in and shut the lid. Then the six men came and carried him away again. “I just can’t manage to shudder,” he said. “I’ll never learn it here, not as long as I live.”

Then a man came in who was taller than all the others and looked terrifying. He was old, though, and had a long white beard. “You wretch,” he cried, “you’re about to learn what it is to shudder, because you’re going to die.” “Not so fast,” the young man replied. “If I’m to die, I’ll have a say in it.” “I’ll have you in my grip in no time,” said the fiend. “Easy now, easy, don’t talk so big. I’m as strong as you are, maybe stronger.” “We’ll see about that,” said the old man. “If you’re stronger, I’ll let you go. Come, let’s test it.” He led him through dark passages to a blacksmith’s forge, took an axe and drove an anvil into the ground with a single blow. “I can do better than that,” said the young man, and he went to the other anvil. The old man stood close by to watch, and his white beard hung down. The young man grabbed the axe, split the anvil with one blow and caught the old man’s beard in the crack. “Now I’ve got you,” he said. “Now it’s your turn to die.” He seized an iron bar and beat the old man until he groaned and begged him to stop, promising him great riches if he did. The young man pulled out the axe and let him go. The old man led him back into the castle and showed him three chests full of gold in a cellar. “One share of this,” he said, “is for the poor, the second for the king, the third for you.” Just then the clock struck twelve, and the spirit vanished, leaving the young man standing in darkness. “I’ll still be able to find my way out,” he said. He felt around, found the way back to the room, and slept there by his fire. The next morning the king came and said, “Surely you’ve learned what shuddering is by now?” “No,” he answered. “What can it be? My dead cousin was here, and a bearded man came and showed me a pile of money down below, but nobody told me what it is to shudder.” “Then,” said the king, “you have saved the castle, and you shall marry my daughter.” “That’s all very well,” he said, “but I still don’t know what it is to shudder!”

Then the gold was brought up and the wedding was held. But no matter how much the young king loved his wife, and no matter how happy he was, he kept saying, “If only I could shudder, if only I could shudder.” In the end this made her angry. Her chambermaid said, “I’ll find a cure for him. He’ll soon learn what it is to shudder.” She went out to the stream that ran through the garden and had a whole bucketful of gudgeons brought to her. That night, while the young king slept, his wife was to pull the covers off him and pour the bucket of cold water and gudgeons over him, so that the little fish flopped all around him. He woke up and cried, “Oh, what is making me shudder so? What is making me shudder so, dear wife? Ah, now I know what it is to shudder!”
